summary: Defines an architecture for traffic engineering in native IP networks using multiple BGP sessions and PCE-based central control. It introduces the CCDR procedures and identifies needed PCEP extensions.

eli5.summary: A central helper steers traffic along chosen roads using several signalling conversations.

subtitle: Using a central controller to steer traffic along optimal paths in IP networks

tldr.problem: IP routers using standard routing protocols optimize for shortest path, but applications need traffic to follow specific routes to ensure quality of service, avoid congestion, or meet other constraints.
tldr.mechanism: A central Path Computation Element (PCE) computes optimal paths for traffic based on network conditions, then instructs routers via multiple BGP sessions to steer traffic accordingly without changing their basic forwarding behavior.
tldr.outcome: Networks can provide end-to-end traffic assurance and quality of service while maintaining distributed routing protocols. The system supports both standard and priority traffic differentiation.

facts.label: Routing sessions
facts.value: Multiple BGP sessions per router pair

today: RFC 8821 is an Informational RFC that describes CCDR as a research-based approach to traffic engineering in native IP networks. While the approach is not yet standardized for mandatory implementation, it offers operators a way to provide traffic assurance without MPLS. Further PCEP extensions are needed to deliver critical parameters from the PCE to routers.

sections.title: The Problem with Distributed Routing
sections.content:
Standard IP routing protocols like BGP and IGP route traffic along the shortest path without considering application requirements. Some applications need low latency, others need to avoid packet loss, and critical applications need guaranteed bandwidth. A network operator may want to direct traffic along different paths based on these requirements, but standard routing protocols do not provide this level of control.

Traffic engineering systems have historically used mechanisms like MPLS (Multi-Protocol Label Switching) to create explicit paths, but these require significant infrastructure changes. This RFC describes an alternative: use a central controller (a Path Computation Element, or PCE) to compute optimal paths for traffic, then use multiple BGP sessions and standard IP routing to steer traffic along those paths without modifying router forwarding.
sections.eli5: Regular routers just follow the shortest path automatically. This solution uses a smart controller to tell routers which path to use for each type of traffic, keeping traffic flowing smoothly.

sections.title: How CCDR Works
sections.content:
Centralized Control Dynamic Routing (CCDR) combines a central PCE controller with multiple BGP sessions between routers. In a simple topology with two routers and multiple links between them, the approach works like this: establish two separate BGP sessions between the routers using different loopback addresses. Send normal traffic through BGP session 1 and priority traffic through BGP session 2. The PCE tells each router to route BGP session 1 traffic via one physical link and BGP session 2 traffic via a different physical link.

Since BGP controls which prefixes go through which session, and the PCE controls which physical links each session uses, traffic can be split and directed according to requirements. The routers themselves continue using standard IP forwarding; the PCE simply configures the BGP next hops to point to different physical addresses.
sections.eli5: Imagine two mail routes between cities. Session 1 carries normal mail via one road, Session 2 carries express mail via another road. The central controller decides which road each session uses based on traffic conditions.

sections.title: Scaling to Large Networks
sections.content:
In large networks with many routers, creating separate BGP sessions between every pair of routers is impractical. CCDR scales using a Route Reflector (RR), a specialized router that acts as a hub. Every edge router establishes multiple BGP sessions with the Route Reflector using different loopback addresses. The PCE computes the path through the network (for example, R1-R2-R4-R7) and instructs each router on that path to route its BGP session traffic appropriately.

This architecture separates the PCE from the Route Reflector, allowing the PCE to focus on path computation while the RR manages BGP advertisement distribution. The PCE communicates with routers using PCEP (PCE Communication Protocol) to set explicit peer routes.
sections.eli5: Instead of direct connections between all routers, they all connect to a central route reflector. The PCE tells each router on the path how to steer traffic, keeping it on the computed route.

sections.title: Different Traffic, Different Paths
sections.content:
Different applications and traffic classes can require different path characteristics. Latency-sensitive traffic (like gaming or video conferencing) needs the shortest route with minimal delay. Loss-sensitive traffic (like file transfer) needs a path with under-loaded links to minimize retransmission. Jitter-sensitive traffic needs a single, stable path to avoid arrival time variation.

CCDR addresses these by using multiple prefix sets, each associated with a different BGP session and path. A network operator defines which prefixes belong to each traffic class, and the PCE selects appropriate paths. This decouples the physical link usage (which the PCE controls) from the traffic class (which operators define via prefix assignment), providing flexible traffic engineering without router changes.
sections.eli5: Video calls go via the shortest path. Big downloads go via uncrowded paths. Critical calls go via stable, dedicated paths. Each type gets the path it needs.

sections.title: Making CCDR Practical
sections.content:
Deploying CCDR in real networks requires attention to several concerns. The system must be scalable to handle large networks through Route Reflector architecture and efficient PCE algorithms. High availability requires backup PCEs and Route Reflectors with automatic failover. Incremental deployment allows operators to start with a subset of routers and traffic classes, then expand.

Loop avoidance is critical: miscalculated paths could create loops where traffic cycles infinitely. The protocol and implementation must validate path computations carefully. End-to-end path performance monitoring requires the PCE to collect real-time network information about link delays, congestion, and packet loss.
sections.eli5: The system needs backup controllers so it does not break if one fails. It must check paths are correct to avoid loops. It needs to watch how well each path performs to make good decisions next time.
